title: Music Composition and Audio Engineering
answer: Score generation, stem separation, drum programming, mixing and mastering, and generated foley.

children.name: Score Generation and Composition
children.blurb: Score generation and composition covers systems that produce musical notation, MIDI data, or full audio arrangements from a prompt, a melody, a chord progression, or a style description.

children.name: Stem Separation and Restoration
children.blurb: Stem separation and restoration covers the work of pulling a finished recording apart into its component parts, typically vocals, drums, bass and a residual instrumental, and of repairing damage in old or badly captured audio.

children.name: Generative Rhythm and Drum Programming
children.blurb: Generative rhythm and drum programming covers the use of AI systems to create, vary, or complete drum patterns and rhythmic parts for music production.

children.name: Automated Mixing and Mastering
children.blurb: Automated mixing and mastering covers software that balances levels, shapes tone, controls dynamics and prepares a finished track for release with limited or no human intervention.

children.name: Generated Foley and Sound Design
children.blurb: Generated Foley and Sound Design covers the use of AI models to create everyday sound effects, ambiences and layered audio beds for film, television, games and podcasts.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in music composition and audio engineering covers systems that write musical scores, split finished recordings into separate instrument tracks, program drum patterns, apply mixing and mastering processing, and synthesize sound effects for film and games. In practice these tools work on audio waveforms and symbolic notation, learning patterns from large collections of existing music and recordings. Composers use them to draft melodic ideas or full arrangements, engineers use them to isolate a vocal from a stereo mix or clean up a noisy archival tape, and sound designers use them to generate footsteps, rain, or room tone without a recording session. The work is largely assistive: a person sets direction, curates output, and makes the final creative calls. None of it replaces an understanding of harmony, arrangement, or acoustics, and the better tools assume the user has some.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Stem separation is the most settled area, with several systems producing usable four stem splits for remixing and restoration, though bleed and artifacts remain on dense or low quality material. Symbolic score generation can produce coherent short passages in a given style, but long form structure, development, and notation accuracy still need heavy editing. Drum programming and loop generation are widely used and reliable within narrow genres, and automated mixing and mastering tools handle loudness, balance, and basic tonal correction well enough for demos and some releases. Generated foley has improved sharply but still struggles with physical plausibility, sync, and the specific sonic character a director wants. The unresolved problems are musical intent over long spans, transparent handling of training data, and the fact that these systems imitate rather than understand. This site tracks 2000 audio models, and 18 of the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits it follows involve AI music services, which shows how much of the field's direction is being argued in court rather than in the studio.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the pipeline from an idea to a finished, placed sound. Score Generation and Composition is the entry point for anyone starting from notation or a musical sketch, covering how models propose melody, harmony, and arrangement. Stem Separation and Restoration sits next to it for people working backward from existing recordings, whether to remix, sample, or repair damaged audio. Generative Rhythm and Drum Programming narrows to the rhythmic layer, where pattern generation and groove are handled separately from pitch and structure. Automated Mixing and Mastering covers the final processing stage, the balance, dynamics, and loudness decisions that turn a rough mix into something releasable. Generated Foley and Sound Design closes the set by moving from music to sound for picture, covering the synthesis of effects and ambience that sit alongside a score. Read together they describe one chain, and a reader can enter at whichever stage matches the problem in front of them.
